content: Sinusitis, or more accurately referred to as rhinosinusitis, is defined as inflammation of both the nasal cavity and the paranasal sinuses. This terminology is preferred because inflammation of the sinuses rarely occurs without concurrent inflammation of the nasal mucosa. Respiratory tract infections, most commonly the common cold, can lead to inflammation and thickening of the sinus membranes, which in turn can obstruct mucus drainage. These infections may be caused by viruses, bacteria, or fungi. Acute rhinosinusitis (ARS) is characterized by symptomatic inflammation of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses lasting less than four weeks. Acute viral rhinosinusitis (AVRS) typically resolves within 7 to 10 days and is managed symptomatically. In contrast, acute bacterial sinusitis is a complication that arises from a viral upper respiratory infection (URI) or allergic inflammation. It has been observed that approximately 6% to 7% of children presenting with respiratory symptoms are diagnosed with acute sinusitis. Notably, the sinuses located in the forehead (frontal sinuses) do not begin to develop until children are around 9 to 12 years old and are not fully formed enough to become infected until the early teenage years. Therefore, cold-related headaches in younger children are usually not indicative of sinus infections. The most common bacterial pathogens responsible for acute sinusitis include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis. Common Causes of Sinusitis: Viral infections Bacterial infections Fungal infections Allergic sinusitis Nasal polyps Deviated nasal septum Immune system-related diseases that can lead to nasal blockage Dental infections Aspirin sensitivity Prolonged intubation, which can result in nosocomial bacterial sinusitis Nasal trauma Foreign objects in the nose Congenital abnormalities such as cleft palate Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) Cystic fibrosis and immunodeficiency syndromes Immune system problems or antibody deficiencies increase the risk of chronic sinus conditions.
